{{Short description|Result in algebra}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Wedderburn's little theorem''' states that every [[finite set|finite]] [[division ring]] is a [[field (mathematics)|field]]; thus, every finite domain is a field. In other words, for [[finite ring]]s, there is no distinction between [[Domain (ring theory)|domains]], [[division ring]]s and fields.

The [[Artin–Zorn theorem]] generalizes the theorem to [[alternative ring]]s: every finite alternative division ring is a field.<ref>{{cite book | last=Shult | first=Ernest E. | title=Points and lines. Characterizing the classical geometries | series=Universitext | location=Berlin | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=2011 | isbn=978-3-642-15626-7 | zbl=1213.51001 | page=123 }}</ref>

== History ==
The original proof was given by [[Joseph Wedderburn]] in 1905,<ref name="Lam-2001-p204">Lam (2001), [{{Google books|plainurl=y|id=f15FyZuZ3-4C|page=204|text=little}} p. 204]</ref> who went on to prove the theorem in two other ways. Another proof was given by [[Leonard Eugene Dickson]] shortly after Wedderburn's original proof, and Dickson acknowledged Wedderburn's priority. However, as noted in {{Harv|Parshall|1983}}, Wedderburn's first proof was incorrect – it had a gap – and his subsequent proofs appeared only after he had read Dickson's correct proof. On this basis, Parshall argues that Dickson should be credited with the first correct proof.

A simplified version of the proof was later given by [[Ernst Witt]].<ref name="Lam-2001-p204"/> Witt's proof is sketched below. Alternatively, the theorem is a consequence of the [[Skolem–Noether theorem]] by the following argument.<ref>Theorem 4.1 in Ch. IV of Milne, class field theory, http://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/cft.html</ref> Let <math>D</math> be a finite [[division algebra]] with [[Center (ring theory)|center]] <math>k</math>. Let <math>[D:k]=n^{2}</math> and <math>q</math> denote the cardinality of <math>k</math>. Every maximal subfield of <math>D</math> has <math>q^{n}</math> elements; so they are isomorphic and thus are conjugate by Skolem–Noether. But a [[finite group]] (the multiplicative group of <math>D</math> in our case) cannot be a union of conjugates of a proper subgroup; hence, <math>n = 1</math>.

A later "[[Group theory|group-theoretic]]" proof was given by [[Ted Kaczynski]] in 1964.<ref>{{cite journal |jstor = 2312328|title = Another Proof of Wedderburn's Theorem |first = T.J. |last = Kaczynski |journal = [[American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=71 |issue=6 |pages=652–653 |date = June–July 1964 | doi = 10.2307/2312328 }} (Jstor link, requires login)</ref>  This proof, Kaczynski's first published piece of mathematical writing, was a short, two-page note which also acknowledged the earlier historical proofs.

== Relationship to the Brauer group of a finite field ==
The theorem is essentially equivalent to saying that the [[Brauer group]] of a finite field is trivial. In fact, this characterization immediately yields a proof of the theorem as follows: let ''K'' be a finite field. Since the [[Herbrand quotient]] vanishes by finiteness, <math>\operatorname{Br}(K) = H^2(K^{\text{al}}/K)</math> coincides with <math>H^1(K^{\text{al}}/K)</math>, which in turn vanishes by [[Hilbert's theorem 90|Hilbert 90]].  

The triviality of the Brauer group can also be obtained by direct computation, as follows.  Let <math>|K| = q,</math> and let <math>L/K</math> be a finite extension of degree <math>n,</math> so that <math>|L|=q^n.</math> Then <math>\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)</math> is a cyclic group of order <math>n,</math> and the standard method of computing [[Group_cohomology#Group_cohomology_of_a_finite_cyclic_group|cohomology of finite cyclic groups]] shows that
<math display="block"> H^2(L/K) = K^{\times}/N_{L/K}(L^{\times}),</math>
where the norm map <math> N_{L/K}:L^{\times} \to K^{\times} </math> is given by 
<math display="block"> N_{L/K}(\alpha) = \prod_{\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(L/K)} \sigma(\alpha) = \alpha \cdot \alpha^{q} \cdot \alpha^{q^2} \cdots \alpha^{q^{n-1}} = \alpha^{\frac{q^n-1}{q-1}}.</math>
Taking <math>\alpha</math> to be a generator of the cyclic group <math>L^{\times},</math> we find that <math>N_{L/K}(\alpha)</math> has order <math>q-1,</math> and therefore it must be a generator of <math>K^{\times}</math>.  This implies that <math>N_{L/K}</math> is surjective, and therefore  <math>H^{2}(L/K)</math> is trivial.

== Proof ==
Let <math>A</math> be a finite domain. For each nonzero <math>b</math> in <math>A</math>, the two maps
:<math>a \mapsto ab, a \mapsto ba: A \to A</math>
are injective by the [[cancellation property]], and thus, surjective by counting. It follows from elementary group theory<ref>e.g., Exercise 1-9 in Milne, group theory, http://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf</ref>  that the nonzero elements of <math>A</math> form a group under multiplication. Thus, <math>A</math> is a [[division ring]].

Since the [[Center (ring theory)|center]] <math>Z(A)</math> of <math>A</math>  is a field,  <math>A</math> is a [[vector space]] over <math>Z(A)</math> with finite dimension <math>n</math>.  Our objective is then to show  <math>n = 1</math>. If <math>q</math> is the order of <math>Z(A)</math>, then <math>A</math> has order <math>{q}^{n}</math>. Note that because <math>Z(A)</math> contains the distinct elements <math>0</math> and <math>1</math>, <math>q>1</math>. For each <math>b</math> in <math>A</math> that is not in the center, the [[Centralizer and normalizer|centralizer]] <math>{Z}_{b}</math> of <math>b</math> is a vector space over <math>Z(A)</math>, hence it has order <math>{q}^{d}</math> where <math>d</math> is less than <math>n</math>. Viewing <math>{Z(A)}^{*}</math>, <math>A^{*}</math>, and <math>{Z}^{*}_{b}</math> as groups under multiplication, we can write the [[Conjugacy class#Conjugacy class equation|class equation]]
:<math>q^n - 1 = q - 1 + \sum {q^n - 1 \over q^d - 1}</math>
where the sum is taken over the conjugacy classes not contained within <math>{Z(A)}^{*}</math>, and the <math>d</math> are defined so that for each conjugacy class, the order of <math>{Z}^{*}_{b}</math> for any <math>x</math> in the class is <math>{q}^{d} - 1</math>. In particular, the fact that <math>{Z}^{*}_{b}</math> is a subgroup of <math>A^{*}</math> implies that <math>q^d-1</math> divides <math>q^n-1</math>, whence <math>d</math> divides <math>n</math> by [[elementary algebra]].

<math>{q}^{n} - 1</math> and <math>q^{d} - 1</math> both admit [[polynomial factorization]] in terms of [[cyclotomic polynomial]]s <math>\Phi_f(q)</math>. The cyclotomic polynomials on <math>\Q</math> are in <math>\Z[x]</math>, and satisfy the identities
:<math>x^n-1 = \prod_{m\mid n} \Phi_m(x)</math> and <math>x^d-1 = \prod_{m\mid d} \Phi_m(x)</math>.

Since each <math>d</math> is a proper divisor of <math>n</math>,
:<math>\Phi_n(x)</math> divides both <math>{x}^{n} - 1</math> and each <math>{x^n - 1 \over x^d - 1}</math> in <math>\Z[x]</math>,

thus by the class equation above, <math>\Phi_n(q)</math> must divide <math>q - 1</math>, and therefore by taking the [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]],
:<math>|\Phi_n(q)| \leq q-1</math>.

To see that this forces <math>n</math> to be <math>1</math>, we will show
:<math>|\Phi_n(q)| > q-1</math>

for <math>n>1</math> using factorization over the complex numbers. In the polynomial identity
:<math>\Phi_n(x) = \prod (x - \zeta),</math>

where <math>\zeta</math> runs over the primitive <math>n</math>-th roots of unity, set <math>x</math> to be <math>q</math> and then take absolute values
:<math>|\Phi_n(q)| = \prod |q - \zeta|.</math>

For <math>n>1</math>, we see that for each primitive <math>n</math>-th [[root of unity]] <math>\zeta</math>,
:<math>|q-\zeta| > |q-1|</math>

because of the location of <math>q</math>, <math>1</math>, and <math>\zeta</math> in the complex plane. Since <math>q \geq 2</math>, the term <math>q-1</math> is at least <math>1</math>. Thus
:<math>|\Phi_n(q)| > q-1.</math>
